title: Research Methods and Scientific Writing
description: The research process, study designs, measurement and bias, research ethics, and writing proposals, reports and references — for final-year projects and beyond.

topics.title: The Research Process and Literature Review
topics.summary: Steps in research, identifying a problem, objectives, hypotheses and reviewing literature.

notes.b: Research is systematic inquiry to generate new knowledge. The process: identify a problem; review the literature; state the aim, specific objectives (SMART) and research questions or hypotheses; choose a design; define the population, sample and sampling method; develop data collection tools; obtain ethical approval; collect data; analyse; interpret; report and disseminate. The PICO framework (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome) helps frame clinical questions. Variables: the independent variable is manipulated or presumed cause; the dependent variable is the outcome; confounders are associated with both and distort the relationship.
k: Problem → literature → objectives → design → ethics → data → analysis → report

notes.b: A literature review summarises and critically appraises existing knowledge, identifies gaps and justifies the study. Sources: primary (original research articles), secondary (reviews, textbooks) and grey literature (reports, theses). Databases include PubMed/MEDLINE, Cochrane Library, Google Scholar and African Journals Online (AJOL). Search strategies use keywords, Boolean operators (AND narrows, OR broadens, NOT excludes) and MeSH terms. Evidence hierarchy places systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomised controlled trials at the top, followed by RCTs, cohort studies, case–control studies, case series, and expert opinion at the bottom.
k: Top of evidence hierarchy: systematic reviews/meta-analyses

topics.title: Study Designs
topics.summary: Descriptive and analytical observational studies, experimental designs and their strengths.

notes.b: Descriptive studies (case reports, case series, cross-sectional surveys) describe the distribution of disease by person, place and time and generate hypotheses. A cross-sectional study measures exposure and outcome at the same time and gives prevalence but cannot establish temporality. A case–control study starts with people with the disease (cases) and without (controls) and looks back at exposures; it is efficient for rare diseases, uses the odds ratio, but is prone to recall bias. A cohort study follows exposed and unexposed people forward to see who develops disease; it gives incidence and relative risk, establishes temporality, suits rare exposures, but is costly and long (prospective) and subject to loss to follow-up.
k: Case–control: rare diseases, odds ratio, recall bias

notes.b: In a randomised controlled trial (RCT), participants are randomly allocated to intervention or control; randomisation balances known and unknown confounders. Blinding (single, double, triple) reduces performance and assessment bias; allocation concealment prevents selection bias. Analysis by intention-to-treat keeps participants in their assigned groups. Other designs: crossover trials, cluster randomised trials (randomising communities or schools), and quasi-experimental studies (no randomisation). Qualitative research (in-depth interviews, focus group discussions, observation) explores meanings and experiences and uses purposive sampling to data saturation.

Exposure and outcome are measured at one point in time.

topics.title: Measurement, Validity and Bias
topics.summary: Questionnaires, reliability and validity, types of bias and sample size.

notes.b: Data collection tools include questionnaires (self-administered or interviewer-administered), interviews, observation checklists, clinical measurements and laboratory tests. Questions may be closed-ended (easy to analyse) or open-ended (rich detail). Tools should be pre-tested (piloted) on a similar population. Reliability is consistency (test–retest, inter-rater reliability, internal consistency measured by Cronbach's alpha, acceptable if ≥ 0.7). Validity is whether the tool measures what it is intended to measure (face, content, construct, criterion validity). Internal validity refers to whether the study's results are true for its sample; external validity (generalisability) to whether they apply to other populations.

Bias is systematic error. Selection bias arises from how participants are chosen (e.g. hospital-based samples, non-response, loss to follow-up). Information (measurement) bias arises from how data are collected (recall bias, interviewer bias, observer bias, social desirability bias). Confounding is addressed by randomisation, restriction, matching, stratification and multivariable analysis. Random error is reduced by larger samples. Sample size depends on the expected prevalence or effect size, desired precision, confidence level (usually 95%, z = 1.96) and power (usually 80%); for a prevalence study, Cochran's formula n = z²p(1−p)/d² is often used, then adjusted for non-response.
k: Control confounding: randomise, match, stratify, adjust

topics.title: Research Ethics
topics.summary: Ethical principles, informed consent, vulnerable groups, ethics committees and research misconduct.

notes.b: Ethical research is guided by the Nuremberg Code (1947, after Nazi experiments — voluntary consent is essential), the Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association, 1964, revised), and the Belmont Report (1979) principles: respect for persons (autonomy and protection of those with diminished autonomy), beneficence (maximise benefits, minimise harm) and justice (fair selection and distribution of burdens and benefits). The Tuskegee syphilis study (USA, 1932–1972) and the Pfizer Trovan trial in Kano (1996) are cited examples of unethical research.

Informed consent must be voluntary, given by competent participants with adequate information (purpose, procedures, risks, benefits, alternatives, confidentiality, the right to withdraw without penalty) and documented; assent is sought from children with parental consent. Vulnerable groups (children, prisoners, pregnant women, people with mental illness) need extra protection. Protocols must be approved by a research ethics committee — in Nigeria, the National Health Research Ethics Committee (NHREC) and registered institutional committees under the National Code of Health Research Ethics (2007). Research misconduct includes fabrication, falsification and plagiarism (FFP). Data must be kept confidential and anonymised where possible.

topics.title: Writing Proposals, Reports and References
topics.summary: Structure of a proposal and thesis (IMRaD), abstracts, referencing styles and presenting results.

notes.b: A research proposal typically contains title, introduction/background, problem statement, justification, aims and objectives, research questions or hypotheses, literature review, methodology (design, setting, population, sampling, sample size, data collection, analysis, ethics), work plan, budget and references. Scientific papers follow IMRaD: Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion, preceded by an abstract (structured: background, methods, results, conclusion; usually 250–300 words). Results are reported objectively using tables and figures; the discussion interprets findings, compares them with other studies, and acknowledges limitations. Past tense is used for methods and results.

References acknowledge sources and allow readers to find them. Common styles: Vancouver (numbered in order of citation — widely used in medical journals) and Harvard/APA (author–date in text, alphabetical reference list). Reference managers (Mendeley, Zotero, EndNote) automate citation. Tables should be self-explanatory with titles above; figures have captions below. Avoid plagiarism by quoting, paraphrasing and citing; similarity checks (e.g. Turnitin) are used by many universities. Findings should be disseminated to stakeholders and communities, through conferences and peer-reviewed publications.
k: Table titles above; figure captions below
